_link.title: I can express reaction rate mathematically using change in concentration divided by change in time

toLevel2.stem: Which formula correctly expresses reaction rate?
In the rate formula, what does Δc represent?
In the rate formula, what does Δt represent?
What are the typical units for reaction rate when using concentration and time?
What does the Δ symbol represent in Δc and Δt?
distractors: A fixed value of a quantity
The total amount of a quantity
The initial value of a quantity

toLevel2.stem: Reaction rate is calculated by dividing the change in concentration by the change in time.
The formula for reaction rate is Rate = Δt / Δc.
Reaction rate equals the change in {{blank:1}} divided by the change in {{blank:2}}.
The mathematical expression for reaction rate is Rate = {{blank:1}} / {{blank:2}}.
The units for reaction rate are typically {{blank:1}} per {{blank:2}} per second.

toLevel3.stem: Why is the formula Rate = Δc / Δt useful in chemistry?
toLevel3.answer: It allows rates to be compared quantitatively between experiments
distractors: It measures the total amount of product formed at the end
It determines the activation energy of the reaction precisely
It identifies whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic

toLevel3.stem: If the concentration of a reactant decreases from 1.0 M to 0.6 M over 20 seconds, what is the change in concentration (Δc)?
Why can mass or volume be used instead of concentration in the rate formula?
toLevel3.answer: Any measurable quantity that changes over time can indicate rate
distractors: Mass and volume are always more accurate than concentration
Concentration cannot be measured in any chemical reaction
Mass and volume do not change during a chemical reaction

toLevel3.stem: What does a larger value of Δc / Δt indicate about a reaction?
toLevel3.answer: The reaction is proceeding at a faster rate
distractors: The reaction is proceeding at a slower rate
The reaction has a higher activation energy
The reaction produces more heat per second

toLevel3.stem: A student calculates a rate using change in mass instead of change in concentration. When would this substitution be appropriate?
toLevel3.answer: When a gas is produced and escapes an open system
distractors: When all reactants are in aqueous solution only
When the reaction occurs in a sealed container
When no gas is produced during the reaction

toLevel3.stem: Why does Rate = Δc / Δt give an average rate rather than an instantaneous rate?
toLevel3.answer: It measures the change over a time interval, not at a single point
distractors: It only works for reactions that occur at constant speed
It measures the maximum rate during the entire reaction
It ignores the concentration of the products entirely

toLevel3.stem: The rate formula Δc / Δt can also be adapted to use change in mass or volume divided by change in time.
A larger value of Δc / Δt indicates a {{blank:1}} reaction rate, while a smaller value indicates a {{blank:2}} rate.
The formula Rate = Δc / Δt gives an {{blank:1}} rate over a time interval, not an {{blank:2}} rate at a single point.
When a gas is produced in an open system, the change in {{blank:1}} over time can be used instead of {{blank:2}} to calculate rate.

toLevel4.stem: A reactant concentration drops from 0.80 mol L⁻¹ to 0.50 mol L⁻¹ over 30 seconds. What is the average rate?
A product concentration increases from 0.00 mol L⁻¹ to 0.20 mol L⁻¹ in 10 seconds. What is the average rate of product formation?
In an experiment, the mass of a reaction flask decreases from 150.0 g to 148.5 g over 60 seconds as gas escapes. What is the average rate of mass loss?
A student measures a reactant concentration of 0.60 mol L⁻¹ at t = 0 s and 0.36 mol L⁻¹ at t = 40 s. What is the average rate?
Two experiments have rates of 0.05 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ respectively. Which experiment has the faster reaction?
toLevel4.answer: The first experiment with a rate of 0.05 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
distractors: The second experiment with a rate of 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
Both experiments have the same reaction rate
The rates cannot be compared without knowing Ea

toLevel4.stem: A gas is collected at a rate of 12 mL in 60 seconds. What is the average rate of gas production?
A reaction has a rate of 0.04 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. How much will the reactant concentration decrease in 25 seconds?
If concentration drops from 0.90 M to 0.60 M in 15 seconds, Δc = {{blank:1}} M and the rate = {{blank:2}} mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
A flask loses 3.0 g of mass over 120 seconds as gas escapes. The average rate of mass loss is {{blank:1}} g s⁻¹, calculated using Δ{{blank:2}} / Δt.
To compare two experiments quantitatively, a student calculates the {{blank:1}} for each using the formula Δc / {{blank:2}}.

toLevel5.stem: A student calculates the average rate over 60 seconds as 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. The instantaneous rate at t = 5 s is 0.05 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Why are these values different?
toLevel5.answer: The rate decreases over time, so the early instantaneous rate is higher than the average
distractors: The student made an error in the instantaneous rate calculation
Average rate is always higher than instantaneous rate at any point
The formula Δc / Δt cannot be used for average rate calculations

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that Rate = Δc / Δt gives the exact rate of reaction at every moment. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — it gives an average rate over the interval, not the rate at each moment
distractors: Correct — the formula always gives the exact instantaneous rate
Incorrect — the formula measures activation energy, not rate
Correct — rate is constant throughout any chemical reaction

toLevel5.stem: Two students measure the rate of the same reaction. Student A uses Δc / Δt over the first 10 seconds. Student B uses Δc / Δt over the first 60 seconds. Whose calculated rate will be higher?
toLevel5.answer: Student A, because the rate is fastest at the start of the reaction
distractors: Student B, because a longer time interval gives a higher rate
Both will get the same rate because the reaction is identical
Student B, because more data points improve the calculation

toLevel5.stem: A student uses change in gas volume instead of concentration to calculate rate. Under what condition would this be an unreliable measure?
toLevel5.answer: If the system is open and some gas escapes before being collected
distractors: If the reaction produces a gas as one of its products
If the reaction takes place at constant temperature throughout
If the gas produced is heavier than air in the surroundings

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'A reaction with Δc = 0.5 M and Δt = 50 s is always faster than one with Δc = 0.3 M and Δt = 50 s.' Is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — a larger Δc over the same Δt gives a higher rate
distractors: No — the reaction with smaller Δc is always faster
No — rate cannot be compared without knowing the Ea values
Yes — but only if both reactions are exothermic

toLevel5.stem: An experiment records concentration at t = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 seconds. The average rates calculated for each 10-second interval get progressively smaller. What does this pattern reveal?
toLevel5.answer: The reaction slows down as reactants are consumed
distractors: The measuring equipment is becoming less accurate over time
The activation energy is increasing as the reaction proceeds
The reaction is speeding up as more product is being formed

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that using smaller time intervals (e.g., 1-second) to calculate Δc / Δt gives values closer to the true instantaneous rate. Is this reasoning sound?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — smaller intervals better approximate the tangent to the curve
distractors: No — smaller intervals always give less accurate rate values
No — the time interval has no effect on the calculated rate
Yes — but only if the reaction is occurring in a closed system

toLevel5.stem: A reaction produces CO₂ gas. A student monitors rate using mass loss in an open flask and concentration change in a closed flask. How would the calculated rates compare?
toLevel5.answer: They should give comparable rates if both methods are measuring the same reaction accurately
distractors: Mass loss always gives a higher rate than concentration change
Concentration change always gives a higher rate than mass loss
The two methods cannot be used for the same reaction

toLevel5.stem: Calculating Δc / Δt over a shorter time interval gives a value closer to the {{blank:1}} rate because it better approximates the {{blank:2}} to the concentration-time curve.
When average rates decrease over successive time intervals, it shows the reaction is {{blank:1}} as the {{blank:2}} concentration decreases.
